newsitem.title: INDIA: India set to import wheat to check rising prices.
newsitem.headline: India set to import wheat to check rising prices.

text.p: India may have to import wheat to augment domestic supplies and rein in spiralling prices despite its current status as a net exporter, analysts and traders said on Wednesday.
"Chances are fair that India may go for imports," said Tarun Kumar, of Space Group, a leading Delhi-based foodgrain trader.
"The government is considering import of one million tonnes of wheat as a short-term measure to arrest the spiralling wheat prices," the Economic Times daily reported on Wednesday.
The imported wheat would be used for re-export and help check rising prices, it quoted State Trading Corp (STC) chairman B.K. Chaturvedi as saying.
The report could not be independently confirmed.
"One million tonnes is very high. It may not be possible. Maybe imports could be 200,000-300,000 tonnes," Kumar said.

India last imported two million tonnes of wheat in 1991/92 (April/March). It exported 600,000 tonnes of the cereal in 1995/96 and 1.07 million tonnes up to September 30 this year, when the government halted exports.
Kumar said the import quantity would depend on the buffer the government would like to build, but would be much lower than one million tonnes.
Analysts said even without imports domestic prices should start falling in February since the new crop is due in March.
India expects a wheat crop of about 64 million tonnes in 1997. A clear picture should emerge by early February.
"I do not think they (government) will import in a large way. They may import 100,000-150,000 tonnes," said Prem Garg, another leading Delhi trader.
Dwindling government reserves have caused wheat prices to rise sharply in recent months compared to prices last year.
"There is a 40 percent increase in prices in six months," Garg said.
He said domestic wheat prices were already declining, with semi hard wheat quoted on Wednesday at 6,700 rupees per tonne compared to 7,500 rupees last week.
Garg said a similar quality of wheat had been priced at 5,200 rupees per tonne at the same time last year.
Some analysts say growers are holding on to their stocks in order to drive up prices further, and later sell to the government for a larger profit.
Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav said on Tuesday that state governments had been asked to take stringent action against hoarders under India's Essential Commodities Act.
Yadav said the government would, if necessary, raise the quantity of wheat sold in the open market every month from government stocks to check prices.
Government wheat procurement in the 1995/96 growing season fell to 8.2 million tonnes against 12.3 million tonnes the previous year due to a three million tonne shortfall in output.
As of October 1, the state-run Food Corporation of India held 19.6 million tonnes of foodgrain -- wheat, rice and other cereals -- down from 29.9 million tonnes a year earlier.
But October stocks were well above the buffer norm set by the government of 16.6 million tonnes.
Foodgrain stocks have fallen steadily from 25.27 million tonnes in July, down from 32.01 million tonnes in August 1995.
